Who gets to arrive? Investigating Australia’s migration stories

Immigration Museum (Old Customs House), Melbourne

Purpose of this site

This digital learning resource is designed for primary educators and Year 6 students exploring Australian migration histories at the Immigration Museum (Old Customs House, Melbourne). Grounded in the Australian Curriculum (Version 9.0) HASS strands History and Civics & Citizenship, this site bridges on-site fieldwork with inquiry-driven classroom learning. By examining primary source documents, material culture, and personal oral histories, students investigate 20th-century push and pull factors, historical entry policies, and Australia's evolving multicultural identity. This resource provides classroom-ready inquiry experiences and curated digital and physical tools to foster critical historical thinking, intercultural empathy, and active, informed civic participation in young learners.

Page 2 · Site Context Students & Teachers

The Old Customs House: Melbourne’s front door

Located at 400 Flinders Street along the banks of the Yarra River (Birrarung), the historic Old Customs House was constructed between 1855 and 1876 as Melbourne’s primary maritime gateway. Architecturally designed in the grand Renaissance Revival style, the building historically operated as the imperial administrative hub for processing trade tariffs, inspecting imported cargo, and registering passenger arrivals. As the principal port of entry during the Victorian gold rush and post-Federation era, it played a pivotal role in enforcing national immigration legislation, including the Immigration Restriction Act 1901. In 1998, this civic landmark was repurposed into the Immigration Museum to preserve, commemorate, and interpret Australia’s complex migration heritage. Today, the museum’s historic Long Room and galleries house primary artefacts, oral histories, and interactive exhibitions that engage Year 6 students in investigating 20th-century push and pull factors, historical entry policies, and the evolving multicultural identity of contemporary Australian society.

Curriculum alignment

This digital learning resource aligns directly with the Year 6 Australian Curriculum: HASS (Version 9.0) focus on “Australia in the past and present, and its connections with a diverse world”. Designed for primary educators, this unit integrates History and Civics & Citizenship through an inquiry-driven study of 20th-century migration to the Immigration Museum (Old Customs House). By interrogating primary source documents, oral histories, and material culture, Year 6 students analyse push and pull factors, changing government selection policies, and the evolving nature of Australian citizenship. Through authentic place-based fieldwork, students develop critical HASS inquiry skills, evaluate ethical historical decisions, and build intercultural empathy.

Word count: 103 words
📋

Australian Curriculum (Version 9.0) Alignment

1. Content Descriptions (Knowledge & Understanding)

AC9HS6K03 History

“the motivation of people migrating to Australia since Federation and throughout the 20th century, their stories and effects on Australian society, including migrants from the Asia region”

Unit focus: Investigating push and pull factors (e.g., post-WWII European migration, post-1975 refugee arrivals), personal luggage artefacts, and oral histories.

AC9HS6K02 History – Citizenship

“changes in Australia’s political system and to Australian citizenship after Federation and throughout the 20th century that impacted First Nations Australians, migrants, women and children”

Unit focus: Examining legislative policy shifts at the Old Customs House, including the Immigration Restriction Act 1901 (Dictation Test), the Nationality and Citizenship Act 1948, and the 1967 Referendum.

2. HASS Inquiry Skills

AC9HS6S01 Questioning & Researching

Posing probing, open-ended, and ethical inquiry questions before, during, and after fieldwork to guide historical investigations.

AC9HS6S04 AC9HS6S07 Evaluating & Communicating

Analysing primary and secondary sources (documents, exhibition panels, artefacts) to identify perspectives, draw evidence-based conclusions, and record digital narratives.

🌏

Cross-Curriculum Priorities

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures

Focus: Examining First Nations perspectives on 20th-century federal immigration policies, continuous connection to Country/Place, and the ongoing struggle for civil rights and citizenship (e.g., the 1962 federal vote and 1967 Referendum).

Asia and Australia’s Engagement with Asia

Focus: Tracing post-WWII and post-1975 Asian migration journeys, analysing push/pull factors, and celebrating the rich cultural contributions of Asian-Australian communities.

🧠

General Capabilities

Intercultural Understanding Level 4

Focus: Reflecting on personal and collective cultural identities, interrogating cultural labels and stereotypes, and applying perspective-taking to foster mutual respect and empathy across diverse communities.

Ethical Understanding Level 4

Focus: Evaluating the social justice implications, moral fairness, and human rights impacts of historical entry restrictions (such as the Dictation Test) versus contemporary multicultural policies.

Learning experiences & resources

Two classroom-ready experiences that take students from their own family stories to the evidence on the museum walls, supported by four annotated resources.

Experience 1 · Before the visit Experience 2 · At the museum Annotated resources Photos
1
Learning Experience 1

Pre-Visit Orientation – “My Family’s Migration Story”

Inquiry stageTuning In & Framing Questions (Pre-Visit Classroom Orientation)
Target strand & skillsYear 6 History (AC9HS6K03) & HASS Inquiry Skills (AC9HS6S01)
FormatClassroom-Ready Activity Sequence

  1. Family Interview Preparation

    A few days prior to the visit, Year 6 students interview a parent, grandparent, or family friend about their family’s origin story (whether generations ago or recent arrivals). Students record key historical details using a structured interview template: country of origin, approximate era of arrival, and primary motivations for moving, while respectfully acknowledging First Nations Australians’ continuous connection to Country and unceded sovereignty.

  2. Interactive World Mapping

    In class, students place a pin or coloured sticker on a large collaborative world map indicating their family’s geographic place of origin. This interactive visual display acts as a powerful inquiry starter, highlighting spatial interconnections, global migration routes, and illustrating Australia’s contemporary identity as a vibrant, multicultural nation shaped by successive waves of global movement and diverse cultural heritage.

  3. “Push and Pull” Categorisation

    The teacher introduces the core disciplinary concepts of push factors (e.g., conflict, economic hardship, political persecution, environmental change) and pull factors (e.g., employment, safety, family reunification, educational opportunity). Working in small collaborative inquiry teams, students analyse and sort their family’s personal stories, or a provided set of historical migrant case studies, into these two analytical categories to identify common migration patterns over time.

  4. Material Object Connection

    Students share a photo, sketch, or detailed physical description of one treasured heirloom, document, or memento their family brought with them or kept to remember “home.” This personal connection primes students to critically engage with the physical material culture, personal luggage displays, and primary object tags during their upcoming fieldwork at the Immigration Museum, connecting emotional resonance with historical evidence.

  5. Pre-Visit Question Wall

    Students formulate open-ended, ethical inquiry questions they are curious to investigate during their museum field trip (e.g., “What did 20th-century migrants pack in their trunks?” or “How did entry policies decide who could settle?”). These student-led questions are posted on a classroom “Inquiry Wall” using graphic organisers, providing clear learning goals to guide on-site research and frame post-visit reflections.

Word count: 358 words
2
Learning Experience 2

On-Site Museum Fieldwork – “Passing the Test: Interrogating Historical Inclusion”

Inquiry stageFinding Out & Primary Source Analysis (On-Site Museum Fieldwork)
Target strand & skillsYear 6 History (AC9HS6K03 & AC9HS6K02) and HASS Inquiry Skills (AC9HS6S04)
FormatClassroom-Ready Activity Sequence

  1. Gallery Exploration (Getting In Gallery)

    Student inquiry teams navigate the museum’s Getting In gallery to investigate how 20th-century Australian immigration selection policies systematically determined who could enter, settle, and gain citizenship. Assigned cooperative inquiry roles (e.g., Lead Researcher, Primary Source Analyst, Media Photographer), student teams examine interactive exhibition panels detailing legislative changes following Federation, evaluating cause, effect, and historical continuity (AC9HS6K02, AC9HS6K03).

  2. Primary Source Inspection

    Working in small groups, students conduct a rigorous inspection of authentic primary source artefacts and document facsimiles on display under glass. These include original handwritten 1900s Dictation Test passages administered in obscure European languages, post-WWII Assisted Passage Scheme applications, White Australia Policy political pamphlets, and historical migrant registration cards. Students record key textual evidence, identifying who authored each document and whose voice is excluded (AC9HS6S04).

  3. Harvard Project Zero Routine (Circle of Viewpoints)

    Students select one specific historical policy document or artefact and complete a structured “Circle of Viewpoints” matrix, either digitally on iPads using this site’s Circle of Viewpoints tool or on printed copies on their clipboards. Teams analyse the historical entry scenario from three contrasting perspectives, evaluating power dynamics and moral implications:

    The Customs/Immigration Officer:Enforcing administrative rules, trade tariffs, and official exclusion laws at the historic Old Customs House port.
    A Migrant Seeking Entry:Navigating foreign language dictation tests, official restrictions, family separation, and emotional push/pull factors.
    A Community Advocate/Civil Rights Activist:Arguing for human rights, procedural fairness, ethical reform, and democratic inclusion.

    Open the digital Circle of Viewpoints tool →

  4. Evaluative Discussion in the Long Room

    Student groups gather in the grand, historic Long Room, the precise location where customs officials historically processed passenger paperwork, to participate in a teacher-facilitated evaluative Socratic discussion. Guided by the central inquiry prompt: “How did government policies create systemic barriers to inclusion, and how did migrants navigate these rules to contribute to Australian society?”, students share perspective evidence and reflect on ethical civic agency.

  5. Inquiry Wall Update & Fieldwork Journaling

    Students capture high-resolution photographic evidence of gallery exhibits and record primary source quotes in their physical fieldwork booklets. These findings directly answer the student-generated inquiry questions from their classroom “Question Wall” during Experience 1, preparing teams to synthesise their findings into post-visit digital storytelling projects (AC9HS6S07).

Annotated supporting resources

Digital / web-based resources

Resource 1Digital

Museums Victoria Collections – Migration & Diversity Online Portal

Interactive Web Database & Digital Archive

This official digital archive provides high-resolution 3D object scans, primary photographs, and oral history clips from the Immigration Museum’s permanent collection. In the classroom, Year 6 students use this digital portal during pre-visit orientation (Experience 1) to inspect 20th-century migrant luggage, passenger logs, and personal heirlooms. Digitally interacting with material culture prior to the trip builds baseline historical empathy and activates prior knowledge (AC9HS6K03). Post-visit, students revisit these digital artefacts to re-examine gallery details, supporting multimodal inquiry for diverse learners and connecting physical museum displays directly to classroom-based research.

Museums Victoria Collections ↗Immigration Museum ↗
Word count: 112 words
Resource 2Digital

National Archives of Australia (NAA) – Immigration and Citizenship Records

Government Digital Primary Source Archive

The National Archives digital portal grants students direct access to digitised 20th-century primary records, including post-WWII migrant selection cards, assimilation pamphlets, and historical arrival photographs. This tool allows Year 6 inquiry teams to examine authentic historical evidence of government policy changes following Federation (AC9HS6K02). By comparing official government landing records with personal oral histories, students evaluate cause, effect, and historical perspective (AC9HS6S04). This digital portal bridges macro-level national policy with micro-level human experiences, empowering students to interrogate how federal laws historically controlled entry and defined Australian citizenship.

NAA: Immigration and citizenship ↗NAA: Migrant stories ↗
Word count: 112 words

Physical / text / visual resources

Resource 3Physical / visual

The Dictation Test (1901–1958) – Listening Booth & Primary Source Reproductions

On-Site Museum Interactive & Primary Source Set

This interactive museum installation and primary document display allows Year 6 students to experience the Dictation Test firsthand by listening to authentic 1920s audio prompts and attempting to transcribe 50-word passages on booth notepads. Interacting with this exhibit and its accompanying archival reproductions provides a powerful sensory and ethical hook. Students evaluate how foreign language tests were strategically manipulated by customs officers to restrict non-European entry (AC9HS6K02), fostering deep ethical inquiry into historical exclusion, administrative power, and legislative discrimination (AC9HS6S04).

Word count: 107 words
Resource 4Physical / visual

Shaun Tan’s Graphic Novel The Arrival (2006)

Wordless Picture Book / Visual Literature

Shaun Tan’s wordless graphic novel The Arrival depicts a migrant’s emotional journey to a surreal, foreign land, capturing the universal disorientation, hope, and resilience of leaving home. Used during classroom pre- and post-visit lessons, this visual text scaffolds historical empathy for students of all reading abilities. Through detailed visual inquiry, Year 6 students analyse wordless narrative cues to explore universal push and pull factors (AC9HS6K03). Pairing Tan’s visual literature with physical museum artefact displays deepens students’ intercultural understanding, encouraging them to appreciate the shared human experiences and emotional motives behind global migration stories.

Page 6 · Critical Reflection Teacher Page

Critical reflection: Why this place matters for HASS

Place-Based Learning and Disciplinary Conceptual Understanding

Integrating a place-based site study at the Immigration Museum (Old Customs House) transforms abstract curriculum content into an authentic, relational investigation of place, space, and human movement (Preston, 2015; Smith, 2002). Rather than treating local sites as static “containers for factual details” (Preston, 2015, p. 47), immersive fieldwork at this historic maritime gateway grounds Year 6 History (AC9HS6K03) and its citizenship focus (AC9HS6K02) in tangible, real-world human experiences. By stepping into the historic Long Room where customs officers once processed trade and arrivals, students directly connect physical spaces with abstract legislative concepts, institutional power, and administrative control. Experiencing this primary contact zone allows primary students to examine how federal government policies historically regulated entry, granted citizenship, and shaped Australia’s multicultural identity over time (Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority [ACARA], 2022). Drawing on Preston’s (2015) relational geography framework, interrogating the local physical environment alongside broader national and global scales enables Year 6 learners to analyse the complex push and pull factors driving 20th-century migration, ultimately developing sophisticated disciplinary understandings of spatial interconnection, cause and effect, and temporal continuity across history.

The Permeable Classroom, Material Culture, and Historical Empathy

Furthermore, place-based fieldwork exemplifies Taylor et al.’s (2018) concept of the “permeable classroom,” wherein the traditional physical boundaries of school walls dissolve to connect learners directly with authentic community resources, cultural institutions, and living archives. Engaging with original material culture, such as 20th-century migrant trunks, landing permits, and personal keepsakes, bridges the gap between abstract historical evidence and emotional resonance (Taylor et al., 2018). Analysing primary source facsimiles of the Dictation Test alongside personal oral history recordings fosters deep historical empathy, prompting Year 6 learners to navigate the insider and outsider perspectives of historical actors as they reflect on shared experiences of arrival, sacrifice, resilience, and belonging (Kindenberg, 2026; Taylor et al., 2018). This critical engagement with local artefacts and lived experiences helps primary learners recognise that history is constructed through diverse human narratives, shifting students from passive consumers of “hand-me-down curricula” into active, reflective investigators and co-creators of historical knowledge (Preston, 2015; Smith, 2002).

Backward Design and Cultivating Active Civic Agency

To ensure fieldwork achieves enduring conceptual transfer rather than devolving into “activity-oriented” busywork, what Wiggins and McTighe (2005, p. 16) term the “twin sins” of traditional unit design, the unit adopts a Backward Design framework. Aligning on-site primary source investigations with essential inquiry questions ensures student learning remains purposeful, reflective, and intellectually rigorous (“minds-on”) across all stages (Wiggins & McTighe, 2005). Through Wiggins and McTighe’s (2005) facets of understanding, specifically perspective and empathy, students critically evaluate historical exclusionary policies, such as the Immigration Restriction Act 1901, and reflect on contemporary multicultural citizenship in a democratic society. By examining how civic values, democratic rights, and human dignity evolved over time, students critically evaluate contemporary social justice issues and recognise their own personal agency as democratic decision-makers. Ultimately, this site-based HASS inquiry fulfils Goal 2 of the Alice Springs (Mparntwe) Education Declaration (Education Council, 2019) by empowering young Australians to become active, informed, and ethically conscious community members committed to equity, social justice, and democratic inclusion.
